title: Organised crime inside the state
summary:
In Mexico, Honduras and Venezuela, drug-trafficking groups have paid officials from town halls up to the presidency. In April 2026 a Manhattan court indicted the sitting governor of Sinaloa and nine other officials over a protection deal with the Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. Prosecutors allege he met the faction before his election and agreed to appoint officials it approved. Former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández was convicted in New York of cocaine conspiracy; a US presidential pardon later freed him. Venezuela's president, Nicolás Maduro, and senior commanders face US narco-terrorism charges that no court has tested.

In Ecuador and Montenegro, courts have convicted judges who protected traffickers. After investigators decrypted a trafficker's phone, Ecuador's National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants, among them judges, prosecutors and police commanders. A Podgorica court jailed the former president of Montenegro's Supreme Court for 10 years for protecting a smuggling ring led by her son.

In Moldova, about $1 billion was taken from Moldovan banks in 2014 through loans repaid with new loans. Vlad Plahotniuc, who led the Democratic Party, was extradited from Greece and sentenced to 19 years.

In Cambodia, Chen Zhi, founder of the Prince Group conglomerate, advised Hun Sen and other leaders. The US indicted him for fraud and money laundering in 2025.

The groups get protection from arrest and extradition, warnings of police operations, and safe passage for shipments. Many cases came to light in US courts, through decrypted phones, or through wiretaps placed on traffickers.
implications: In these places, a person who reports a trafficker may be reporting to an official the trafficker pays. Judges and prosecutors who take payments shelve cases, so victims and witnesses have no safe court to turn to. Police commanders on a cartel's payroll warn it before raids. Public money is lost as well: Moldova's bank theft equalled about 12% of the country's yearly economic output. Where courts at home do not act, the only trials take place abroad. An official charged in the United States, such as the governor of Sinaloa, can stay in office at home.
uncertain: Several cases rest on US indictments, sanctions or designations that no court has tested, including those against Nicolás Maduro, Haiti's former president Michel Martelly and Colombia's president Gustavo Petro. US intelligence analysts concluded in 2025 that Venezuela's government probably does not have a policy of cooperating with the Tren de Aragua gang.

title: China's long arm abroad
summary: In the Pacific islands, China pays politicians and places police officers inside local forces. In the Solomon Islands, China funded a fund run by the prime minister's office. The prime minister's secretary told a parliamentary hearing that 39 of the 50 MPs received payments from it in 2021. Chinese police advisers have worked with the Solomon Islands police since 2022. Up to a dozen uniformed Chinese officers work alongside Kiribati's police, and China has sent police advisers to Vanuatu. Fiji asked Chinese officers to leave its police force in 2024 but kept its 2011 police agreement with China. In Europe, Hungary agreed in 2024 to let Chinese officers patrol with Hungarian police in tourist areas. Italy ended similar joint patrols in 2022. In Taiwan, a court convicted four former aides of the governing DPP in 2025 of spying for Chinese military intelligence. One had worked for the foreign minister. Taiwanese courts have also jailed people who used money from China to pay for local election campaigns and for trips to China for village chiefs. In the United States, Eileen Wang, mayor of Arcadia, California, pleaded guilty in 2026 to acting as an illegal agent of China. Her former fiancé, who ran her council campaign, is serving four years. Linda Sun, a former deputy chief of staff to New York's governor, has been charged with the same offence and has not been tried. In Canada, a public inquiry found in 2025 that China is the most active foreign state interfering in the country. It worked through the United Front Work Department, a Communist Party body that builds influence among Chinese communities abroad. China gets votes, information and police cooperation over its citizens abroad. Most cases came to light through prosecutions, parliamentary hearings and government inquiries.
implications: In the Pacific islands, MPs who take money from a foreign-funded account can face pressure on how they vote, and residents cannot easily see who paid whom. Where Chinese police work inside local forces, people from China living there can be tracked and sent back. In Fiji in 2017, Chinese police working with local officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals and flew them to China. In Taiwan, the United States and Canada, voters may elect candidates whose campaigns were paid for or directed by another government without knowing it.
uncertain: Claims that China pressed delegations to elect Qu Dongyu as head of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization in 2019 have not been proven. A 2018 report that China's military put spy chips in US server boards was denied by the companies and doubted by US and UK security agencies.

title: Russia's networks in Europe and Africa
summary:
In Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Equatorial Guinea, Russian troops work for the governments. They belong to Africa Corps, a Russian defence ministry unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's African work after Wagner's founder, Yevgeny Prigozhin, died in 2023. About 2,000 Russian troops stayed in Mali after Wagner left in June 2025. In Equatorial Guinea, up to 200 of them protect President Teodoro Obiang. In Togo, a 2025 defence pact lets Russian navy ships dock at the port of Lomé. In the Central African Republic, Wagner fighters have guarded the president since 2018, and reporting links the deployment to gold, diamond and timber concessions.

In Belarus, Russian forces launched part of the 2022 invasion of Ukraine from Belarusian soil, and a referendum that year allowed permanent Russian bases. In Georgia, the US Treasury sanctioned Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling party, saying he advanced Russia's interests. He made his fortune in Russia. In Moldova, a court jailed the governor of Gagauzia for seven years in 2025 for funding her party with undeclared Russian money.

In Italy and Austria, the Lega and the Freedom Party signed cooperation pacts with United Russia, Vladimir Putin's ruling party. Gerhard Schröder, Germany's former chancellor, chaired the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company. Voice of Europe, a news site in Prague funded from Russia, paid European politicians until Czech intelligence exposed it in 2024. In Britain, former MEP Nathan Gill was jailed in 2025 for taking bribes to make pro-Russian statements. Russia gets bases, mining deals, votes and friendly statements. Most cases came to light through sanctions, intelligence briefings, leaked recordings and trials.
implications: In Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and the Central African Republic, the soldiers who protect the government take orders partly from Moscow. That makes it harder for citizens to change those governments. Where Russian forces are paid in mining concessions, as reporting says happened in the Central African Republic, the income from those mines leaves the country. In Europe, voters may back a party or politician without knowing it has a pact with a foreign ruling party or took foreign money. Ukraine, Latvia and Estonia have cut their Orthodox churches' formal ties to Moscow, which changes how ordinary parishes are run.
uncertain: Several cases rest on sanctions or press reporting rather than court rulings, including the US case against Ivanishvili and the reported payments to Madagascar's 2018 presidential candidates. A Milan judge closed the Lega oil-money case in 2023. A Sofia court acquitted the Bulgarian pro-Russia leader Nikolay Malinov of spying for a Russian state think tank in May 2026.

title: Governments buying officials in other countries

countries.note: The Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department directs 'united front' work among overseas Chinese and foreign elites.

In the 1970s the Korean Central Intelligence Agency and businessman Tongsun Park paid US congressmen ('Koreagate'); the House Fraser subcommittee (1978) also examined the KCIA's use of Sun Myung Moon's organisations.
The Russkiy Mir Foundation (2007) and the Voice of Europe network, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024 for paying European politicians.

summary:
In eastern Congo, Rwanda's army commands the M23 armed group, according to UN experts. M23 took the cities of Goma and Bukavu and appointed new provincial governors. In Belarus, Russia keeps permanent bases and has supplied nuclear-capable missiles, after promising President Lukashenko a large loan following the disputed 2020 election.

In Georgia, Bidzina Ivanishvili made his fortune in Russia, founded the ruling Georgian Dream party and nominates the prime minister. The United States and the three Baltic states sanctioned him for advancing Russia's interests. In Bosnia's Serb entity, Republika Srpska, the police signed a cooperation agreement with Russia's interior ministry.

France chooses officials in two small neighbours. The French president is one of Andorra's two co-heads of state. In Monaco, French magistrates proposed by Paris fill key judicial posts, and France names the police chief.

In Yemen, the leader of a southern council formed with help from the United Arab Emirates sat on the country's ruling council until he fled to the UAE in January 2026. UN monitors found credible evidence that the UAE sent weapons to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary at war with the army.

In Canada, a parliamentary committee reported that some unnamed MPs and senators knowingly took part in foreign interference. Canadian police said Indian government agents used a criminal gang against Sikh activists, and Canada expelled six Indian diplomats. In the United States, a jury convicted Senator Bob Menendez of acting as an agent of Egypt.

The sponsoring states get territory, military bases, friendly votes in foreign parliaments and pressure on their critics abroad. These cases came out through UN expert panels, parliamentary inquiries, sanctions decisions, leaked emails and trials.
uncertain: The cases against Ivanishvili and the UAE's arms flights to Sudan rest on sanctions decisions and UN reports, not court verdicts. Tom Barrack was acquitted and the charges against Eric Adams were dismissed. India and the UAE deny the accusations against them.

US House Subcommittee on International Organizations (Fraser), report, October 1978

implications: In eastern Congo, provincial offices answer to commanders backed by a neighbouring army instead of the national government. Belarus hosts Russian troops and missiles, and its territory was used to launch part of the invasion of Ukraine. Sikh residents of Canada face threats arranged by a foreign government. Canadian voters cannot check which of their representatives took foreign money, because the committee did not name them. When a case ends in acquittal or dismissal, as with Tom Barrack and New York mayor Eric Adams, people are left without a settled account of what happened.

title: Governments inside companies
summary:
In China, Russia, Iran and Turkey, governments own, run or place party officials inside companies. China's Company Law requires a Communist Party unit in any company with three or more party members. The party reported that 73.1% of private companies had one in 2018. ByteDance, which owns TikTok, has an internal party committee, and a state fund holds a board seat in its main Chinese subsidiary.

In Iran, the Revolutionary Guards, the country's ideological military force, control more than 812 companies through their engineering arm, Khatam al-Anbiya. These companies build dams, tunnels and oil and gas fields.

In Russia, the state took over the Russian businesses of Danone and Carlsberg in July 2023 under a presidential decree. A nephew of the Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov was named head of Danone Russia. In Turkey, a state trustee fund took over 784 companies the government said were linked to the Gülen religious movement.

Governments also place people inside foreign companies. North Korea gets its programmers hired abroad under stolen identities, and their wages go to its weapons programmes. One Arizona scheme placed them in more than 300 US companies. Chinese state hackers known as Salt Typhoon got into the networks of at least nine US telecom companies, with access to call records.

From 1970 the US CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned Crypto AG, a Swiss firm that sold cipher machines to more than 120 governments. The two agencies read those governments' coded messages.

The states get money, data, control of networks and a say in company decisions. These cases came out through court cases, leaked files, government announcements and reporting by journalists.
implications: Customers of these companies may be passing data to a government they never chose. Governments that bought Crypto AG machines had their coded messages read for decades. A company that hires a remote programmer can end up paying wages into North Korea's weapons programmes. Phone users in the United States had call records exposed to Chinese state hackers. In Russia, a presidential decree let the state take over foreign-owned businesses. Workers and suppliers of firms taken over by the state in Russia and Turkey now answer to managers the government picked.
uncertain: The 2018 report that Chinese spy chips were added to Supermicro server boards was denied by the companies and by US and UK security agencies. Kaspersky denies the US government's claim that it has ties to Russia's FSB. The concerns about China's State Grid in the Philippine power grid were raised in Senate hearings and have not been proven.

title: Foreign money inside Europe's parliaments
summary: Foreign governments have paid members of the European Parliament, the Council of Europe's assembly and national parliaments to speak and vote for them. In Brussels, Belgian police found bags of cash at the home of Greek MEP Eva Kaili in 2022. Prosecutors charge that Qatar and Morocco paid people in the Parliament, some of it through an NGO called Fight Impunity. Kaili is charged and has not been tried. In 2025 Belgian prosecutors charged four people over gifts and football tickets allegedly given for Huawei, the Chinese telecoms company, in return for political positions. Azerbaijan paid members of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), which monitors elections and human rights. A Milan court jailed former Italian MP Luca Volontè in 2021 for taking Azerbaijani money in return for support in the Assembly. Germany's Bundestag lifted the immunity of two CDU MPs over Azerbaijani money. Russia has paid politicians through a network linked to Viktor Medvedchuk. In Britain, former MEP Nathan Gill was jailed for 10 years in 2025 after admitting he took money from a Ukrainian MP to make pro-Russian statements. German prosecutors are investigating AfD politician Petr Bystron over cash from Voice of Europe, a Russian-funded news site. Hungary convicted a former Jobbik MEP of spying on EU institutions for Russia. In Georgia, the US Treasury sanctioned Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party, in 2024 for advancing Russia's interests. He nominates the prime minister. In Israel, police arrested two aides of Prime Minister Netanyahu in 2025 on suspicion of being paid to promote Qatar. The paying governments get speeches, votes and weaker reports on their own conduct. Most cases came to light through police raids, leaked bank records and court cases.
implications: When a member of parliament is paid by a foreign government, voters lose an honest vote on human rights, trade and security without knowing it. In the Council of Europe's assembly, a paid member worked against a report on political prisoners in Azerbaijan. In Georgia, the party that forms the government was founded by a man whom the United States and three Baltic states have sanctioned. Cases take years, and some accused MEPs kept their seats while prosecutors asked for their immunity to be lifted.
uncertain: A 2010 Council of Europe report said Kosovo's then prime minister, Hashim Thaçi, led former KLA commanders who ran criminal trades. It rested on what it called credible indications, not court findings. Belgian prosecutors later said one MEP named in the Huawei case was a different man with the same name.

title: Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement
roles: Country that handed people over or closed schools
summary:
Since a failed coup in July 2016, Turkey's government has pursued followers of Fethullah Gülen at home and abroad. Gülen was a Turkish preacher whose movement ran schools and businesses in many countries. Turkey calls the movement a terrorist group, 'FETÖ', and blames it for the coup. Inside Turkey, about 150,000 people lost public jobs by decree, including 2,745 judges removed the day after the coup.

In Kenya, four Turkish refugees were sent back to Turkey in October 2024 at Turkey's request. Turkish intelligence had taken Gülen's nephew from Kenya in 2021. In Kosovo, Moldova, Malaysia and Kyrgyzstan, local police or intelligence officers detained Turkish teachers and others and put them on flights to Turkey. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2019 that Moldova's transfer of seven teachers was illegal. Kosovo's prime minister sacked his interior minister and intelligence chief over a similar transfer.

In Senegal, Chad, Niger, Guinea, Somalia, Sudan and Pakistan, governments or courts handed Gülen-run schools to Maarif, a Turkish state foundation. In Azerbaijan the schools went to a company part-owned by the state oil firm.

In Germany, Austria and Belgium, the concern is Diyanet, Turkey's state religious office, which pays imams abroad as Turkish civil servants. After the coup, Diyanet told its imams abroad to gather information on Gülen followers. It gave Turkey's parliament reports from 38 countries. Austria reviewed the residence permits of about 40 such imams in 2018. France banned the Grey Wolves, the youth group of a party in Turkey's governing alliance, in 2020.

Turkey gets critics returned for trial, control of schools and information on Turks abroad. Most cases became public through court rulings, government statements and Turkish state media announcing captures.
implications: Turkish citizens abroad who worked for Gülen schools or businesses can be detained and flown to Turkey with little or no court hearing in the country where they live. Families in Africa and Central Asia saw their children's schools change owner by government order. Muslims at Turkish-run mosques in Germany, Austria and Belgium may pray under an imam employed by the Turkish state. Inside Turkey, a teacher, judge or police officer dismissed by decree lost the job without an individual trial.
uncertain: Turkish courts accepted that the Gülen movement organised the 2016 coup, but the movement denies it. German reporting said prosecutors could not prove that imams of DITIB, Diyanet's German branch, spied for Ankara. Interpol refused 773 Turkish arrest requests on Gülen suspects as political.

title: Churches and movements placing members in the state
summary:
In India, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer group, trained many of the people now in government. Prime Minister Narendra Modi worked as a full-time RSS organiser before the group sent him to the BJP. A press count found that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in his second government had RSS roots.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi belongs to the parliamentary league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby that wants to change the constitution. A press report named 10 of her 19 ministers as members of the same league. The ruling LDP's own survey found that 179 of its lawmakers had ties to the Unification Church. Tokyo courts have since ordered the church dissolved.

In South Korea, a court jailed former first lady Kim Keon-hee for taking a necklace and handbag from the Unification Church. Its leader, Han Hak-ja, was also sentenced for bribery. Prosecutors found that the Shincheonji church signed up tens of thousands of its members to the governing party, and they indicted its founder.

In Brazil, a cross-party evangelical caucus in Congress votes as a bloc on issues its churches care about. Chile's president, José Antonio Kast, is a member of the Catholic Schoenstatt movement. In the United States, the televangelist Paula White heads a new White House Faith Office. Ethiopia's prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, sometimes preaches at a Pentecostal church.

In Turkey, the government blames the Gülen movement, a religious network, for the 2016 coup attempt. It dismissed about 150,000 public employees by decree.

The groups gain laws and appointments that match their aims, and some gain money or legal protection. Most of these ties came out through party surveys, press counts of membership lists and criminal cases.
uncertain: Membership of a lawful religious group or lobby is not wrongdoing, and several membership counts come from press reports, not official lists. Opus Dei says William Barr is not a member. The claims about El Yunque in Mexico's PAN were denied by the party.

implications: Where many ministers share one movement's training or lobby membership, people outside it may find laws on schools, religion and the constitution written without them. Japanese families who gave money to the Unification Church saw lawmakers attend its events for years before courts acted. In South Korea, party primaries were affected by church members signed up in bulk. In Turkey, tens of thousands of police, judges and soldiers lost their jobs over alleged links to the movement.

title: Religious nationalism in power
summary:
In India, Japan, Myanmar and Sri Lanka, members of religious nationalist groups serve in cabinets or have helped write laws.

In India, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer group, is the parent organisation of the governing BJP. Prime Minister Narendra Modi worked as a full-time RSS organiser before the RSS sent him to the BJP. ThePrint counted in 2020 that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers had RSS roots. Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan has been associated with the RSS since his teens.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has served in the Diet members' league of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby that wants to change the constitution. A Communist Party newspaper reported that 10 of her 19 ministers belong to that league. It counted 12 in the league of the Shinto Political League, the political arm of Japan's association of Shinto shrines.

In Myanmar, Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' group, proposed the texts behind four race and religion laws that parliament passed in 2015. The military government dropped sedition charges against the monk Wirathu in 2021 and later gave him one of the country's highest honours.

In Sri Lanka, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed Gnanasara, leader of the Buddhist nationalist group Bodu Bala Sena, to chair a legal reform task force in 2021. In September 2026 the Supreme Court ruled invalid the 2019 presidential pardon that had freed him from a contempt sentence.

In Pakistan, a military court convicted a brigadier and four majors of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned group that seeks a caliphate.

These movements get ministers who share their aims, laws based on their drafts, and pardons. Most of this is public, in membership lists, official appointments and court rulings.
implications: Religious minorities in these countries live under laws and officials shaped by groups that favour the majority religion. In Myanmar, the 2015 laws regulate religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men. In Sri Lanka, a monk later jailed twice over statements about Islam chaired proposals for a single legal code. In Japan, ministers in the Shinto league belong to a body that backs constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine. Belonging to these lawful groups is not a crime. It does tell voters which aims their ministers support.
uncertain: The Japanese counts come from a Communist Party newspaper and press reports of league lists, not from official records. The RSS does not publish membership rolls, so counts of ministers with RSS roots are journalists' estimates.

title: Governments that export religion
roles: Where the mosques or churches are
summary: Turkey, Saudi Arabia, other Gulf states and the Russian Orthodox Church pay for or run religious bodies in other countries, and several European governments have acted against them. Turkey's Diyanet, its state religious directorate, runs over 2,000 mosques abroad, and its imams are Turkish civil servants. After the 2016 coup attempt it told those imams to gather information on followers of the Gülen movement. It then gave the Turkish parliament reports from 38 countries. German prosecutors investigated imams of DITIB, its German branch, for spying, but a court later said this could not be proven. Austria reviewed the residence permits of imams employed by ATIB, Diyanet's Austrian branch. In the Netherlands, a parliamentary inquiry found that donors from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar funded mosques to spread hardline Salafi teaching and influenced the choice of imams. Belgium had lent the Great Mosque of Brussels to Saudi Arabia from 1967 and ended that arrangement in 2018, citing foreign interference. Belgian State Security then found members linked to Moroccan intelligence and to Diyanet in the new body set up to run it. The Russian Orthodox Church under Patriarch Kirill backs Russia's war on Ukraine. Ukraine banned the Russian church in 2024. Latvia made its Orthodox Church independent of any outside church authority. Estonia refused to renew the residence permit of the Moscow Patriarchate's head in the country, calling him a security risk. The UK, Canada and Ukraine sanctioned Kirill in 2022. The sponsoring states get a say over what is preached and who preaches, and information on emigrants and critics. These arrangements came to light through parliamentary inquiries, security service findings and government decisions.
implications: Muslims in Germany, Austria and the Netherlands may pray in mosques where the imam is paid by and reports to a foreign government. People who oppose that government, such as followers of the Gülen movement, risk being reported on to Ankara. Orthodox believers in Ukraine, Latvia and Estonia have seen their churches banned, made to cut ties with Moscow, or lose their bishop. Their governments treat a church that supports Russia's war as a security risk.
uncertain: A German court said prosecutors could not prove that Turkey spied through DITIB imams. Swiss federal police files list Patriarch Kirill as a KGB agent from 1970, but this has not been tested in court.
case_role: Where the mosques or churches are

title: Consultants and lobbyists inside the ministries
summary:
In South Africa, the Zondo Commission found in 2022 that Bain & Company, a US consulting firm, helped President Jacob Zuma and his tax chief take over the tax service. Bain's 2015 restructuring cut the unit that produced a third of tax revenue. McKinsey, another US consultancy, admitted in 2024 that it bribed officials at Eskom, the state power company, and Transnet, the state rail company. KPMG withdrew a report on the tax service that had led to charges against a former finance minister.

In Britain, the four largest accounting firms (Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC) lend staff to the Treasury to help write tax law. A parliamentary committee said in 2013 that these staff can then advise clients on loopholes. In Australia, a PwC partner advising the Treasury on tax-avoidance law shared its confidential plans with at least 53 PwC colleagues.

In France, a Senate inquiry reported in 2022 that consultants hired since 2017 had real influence on policy. Leaked Uber files show that Emmanuel Macron, as economy minister, helped Uber in its fight with French regulators. They also show former EU commissioner Neelie Kroes lobbying Dutch officials for Uber. In Canada, the ethics commissioner found in 2019 that Justin Trudeau broke conflict law by pressing his attorney general on behalf of SNC-Lavalin, an engineering firm facing bribery charges. In Rwanda, the Tony Blair Institute, a London non-profit, staffs strategy units inside the president's office. In Brussels, an EU court ruled in 2025 that the European Commission wrongly refused to release Ursula von der Leyen's texts with Pfizer's chief executive about vaccine contracts.

The firms get contracts, early knowledge of new laws and rules written to suit their clients. Most of this came out through public inquiries, leaked files and court cases.
implications: When the firms that advise companies on tax also help write tax law, their clients can pay less and other taxpayers make up the difference. In South Africa, the tax service lost the unit that brought in a third of its revenue. Public money pays for consulting work that is often unpublished, so voters cannot see who shaped a policy. Rules on ride-hailing, vaccine purchases and tax were discussed in private messages that officials then refused to release.
uncertain: Bain denies that it knowingly helped take over South Africa's tax service. Kroes denies wrongdoing, and the Uber Files show messages, not decisions tested in court. The French Senate inquiry led to a tax-fraud investigation of McKinsey, not a conviction.

title: Global firms buying governments
summary:
Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction company, admitted to US authorities that it paid $788 million in bribes in Latin America and Africa. In Peru, courts sentenced two former presidents over its money. Ecuador's former vice-president Jorge Glas is in prison for taking Odebrecht bribes. In Panama, former president Ricardo Martinelli is on trial by video from asylum in Colombia.

Swiss-based commodity traders bought officials at state oil and mining companies. Glencore pleaded guilty to bribery in Nigeria and four other African states, and it paid Congo $180 million to settle bribery claims. Trafigura pleaded guilty in the United States to bribing officials at Brazil's state oil company, Petrobras. A Swiss court convicted it of bribing an Angolan official.

In South Africa, a judicial inquiry found that ministers and heads of state companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family business. In Mozambique, a shipbuilder paid the former finance minister, Manuel Chang, while state companies took on hidden loans. A US jury convicted him.

In Illinois and Ohio, power companies paid the state House speakers. Commonwealth Edison gave jobs and contracts to associates of Speaker Michael Madigan to win support for its bills. FirstEnergy sent money to Speaker Larry Householder's group in return for a law that rescued its nuclear plants.

US prosecutors have charged India's Adani Group with paying Indian officials for solar contracts, and Kenya then cancelled an Adani airport deal. Erik Prince, who founded Blackwater, now supplies armed contractors to the governments of Haiti, Ecuador and Congo.

The companies get public contracts, laws and protection from investigation. Most cases came out through US and Swiss prosecutions, plea deals and national inquiries.
implications: Bribes are added to the cost of roads, power and oil deals, and the public pays through higher prices and lost revenue. Mozambicans carry debts their parliament never approved. In Ohio, a law that rescued a company's nuclear plants was passed after the company paid the House speaker's group. In Peru and Ecuador, courts found that the leaders who awarded the contracts were the ones paid. Where private armed contractors work beside the police, as in Haiti and Ecuador, residents have fewer ways to hold anyone to account for force used against them.
uncertain: The Adani charges are unproven and the group denies them. Emilio Lozoya, the former head of Mexico's state oil company, has not been tried to a verdict. Lula's Car Wash convictions in Brazil were annulled.

title: Industries inside their regulators
summary:
In South Africa, the United States, Peru, Panama and Japan, companies have paid or placed people inside the bodies that regulate or buy from them.

In South Africa, McKinsey and SAP admitted to US authorities that they bribed officials at Eskom, the state power company, and at other public bodies. McKinsey paid a $122 million penalty. The Zondo inquiry found evidence that the prison contractor Bosasa paid for a former minister's birthday party and groceries.

In the United States, the power company FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to a group around Ohio's House Speaker in return for a law rescuing its nuclear plants. He was sentenced to 20 years. Boeing employees carry out much of the safety certification of Boeing planes on behalf of the Federal Aviation Administration. Reporters found more than 2,100 state laws copied almost entirely from model bills, many written by industry-funded groups.

In Peru and Panama, the Brazilian builder Odebrecht paid presidents' governments. A Lima court sentenced former president Alejandro Toledo to 20 years for taking about $35 million. Panama's Odebrecht trial opened in 2026, with former president Ricardo Martinelli taking part by video from asylum in Colombia.

In Japan, a parliamentary commission found that the nuclear regulator had been captured by TEPCO, the company that ran the Fukushima plant. At UN climate talks, the 2023 and 2024 summits were led by men from the hosts' state oil companies. Fossil fuel lobbyists outnumbered most national delegations at both.

The companies get contracts, weaker rules and laws written in their favour. Most cases came out through US settlements, official inquiries, leaked documents and trials.
implications: People pay for weak oversight with their safety and their taxes. In Britain, the makers of cladding misled the safety-testing system before the Grenfell Tower fire killed 72 people. Two Boeing 737 MAX crashes followed a system in which Boeing staff did much of the certification work. In France, the medicines agency was fined for failing to act on warnings about Mediator, a drug thought to have caused hundreds of deaths. In South Africa, consultants bribed officials at the state power and rail companies for inside information on contracts paid from public money.
uncertain: Some cases rest on reporting or opposition memos, such as the Senate Democratic staff memo on Elon Musk's companies, not on findings. John Perkins's account of inflating forecasts so that countries would borrow was questioned by a 2006 New York Times check. Benjamin Netanyahu's bribery trial in Case 4000 has not ended, and he denies the charges.

title: Criminal money inside banks and firms
summary: Drug gangs and other criminal groups own or use banks, transport firms, fuel stations and building companies to clean their money. In São Paulo, prosecutors charged in 2024 that the PCC, Brazil's largest criminal organisation, laundered money through two city bus companies paid with public funds. The city took both companies over. Brazilian investigators later found PCC money held in about forty investment funds that owned ethanol plants, a port terminal and more than a thousand petrol stations. In Jalisco, Nayarit, Michoacán and Zacatecas, the US Treasury in 2026 named tequila distilleries, agave producers and gas stations as fronts for the CJNG cartel. In Emilia-Romagna, Italy's top court in 2022 confirmed more than 70 convictions tied to the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, which had taken over construction firms. In Reggio Emilia, 80 firms were barred from public contracts in 2024 over 'Ndrangheta ties. Banks are used too. TD Bank pleaded guilty in the United States in 2024 to conspiracy to launder money, and some of its employees took bribes. In Cambodia, the United States and the United Kingdom sanctioned the Prince Group, which runs scam compounds, in 2025. A sitting Cambodian senator's network was sanctioned in 2026. At Antwerp and Rotterdam, where most cocaine seized at EU ports is found, a 2025 EU review concluded from shipment sizes that criminal networks have people working inside the ports. The groups get clean money, public contracts and cover for moving drugs. Most cases came to light through prosecutors' raids, through police who broke into encrypted phone networks such as EncroChat and Sky ECC, and through US Treasury sanctions. A sanction is one government's decision, not a court verdict.
implications: Residents pay when criminal groups own ordinary businesses. In Brazil, drivers bought petrol mixed with methanol at stations prosecutors say the PCC controlled. In São Paulo, hundreds of millions of reais in public money went to bus companies accused of laundering for the PCC. In Reggio Emilia, mafia-linked firms bid for building contracts paid with EU recovery money. In Andorra, customers of a bank shut down for laundering had to prove their own savings were legitimate before they could get them back.
uncertain: In Panama, the founders of Mossack Fonseca, the firm at the centre of the Panama Papers, were acquitted of money laundering in 2024. US charges against the Sky ECC chief executive have not been tried, and he denies them. Raiffeisen Bank International has faced supervisory pressure but no penalty for laundering drug money.

title: Companies inside other companies
summary:
In the Netherlands, the government took control of the chipmaker Nexperia in October 2025. Its owner, Wingtech, is almost 30% traceable to the Chinese state. The Dutch government reportedly acted to stop chip know-how and production moving to China. China then banned exports of Nexperia chips packaged in China. In Australia, a company owned by Ye Cheng, a businessman with close Chinese Communist Party ties, holds a 99-year lease on the Port of Darwin, near a base used by US Marines. Both major parties pledged in 2025 to return it to Australian ownership.

In Taiwan, a court in April 2026 jailed the main defendant for 10 years in a case over former TSMC staff passing chip secrets to Tokyo Electron, a Japanese equipment maker. In South Korea, prosecutors charge that a former Samsung executive used Samsung's factory plans to build a copy plant in China with Chengdu city government money. In the United States, Huawei is on trial for stealing trade secrets from five US companies. A US jury convicted the Chinese firm Sinovel of stealing wind-turbine software from AMSC by recruiting one of its engineers. A US court also found the Israeli spyware firm NSO liable for using WhatsApp's systems to plant spyware on about 1,400 phones.

In Djibouti, Mexico, Indonesia and South Africa, foreign companies paid managers of state companies. Ericsson admitted paying Djibouti Telecom officials, and a former Vitol trader was convicted of bribing officials at Pemex, Mexico's state oil firm. Garuda Indonesia's former chief was jailed for bribes traced to Rolls-Royce and Airbus. ABB admitted paying an Eskom official more than $37 million.

The companies get technology, contracts and control of strategic assets. These cases came to light through prosecutions, lawsuits and government orders.
implications: When a foreign owner or a bribed insider takes a company's technology, the jobs and income built on it can move abroad. AMSC said its losses from the Sinovel theft exceeded US$800 million. When managers of state companies take bribes, the public pays more for planes, power stations and phone networks. Ports and chip plants owned by foreign firms can also become bargaining chips between governments, as when China blocked Nexperia chip exports after the Dutch takeover.
uncertain: The Darwin case rests on the owner's political ties, not on proven misuse, and a 2021 review found no security grounds to cancel the lease. A US judge acquitted Fujian Jinhua of stealing Micron's memory-chip secrets in 2024, though its partner UMC pleaded guilty. The Huawei and Samsung cases have not been decided.

title: Spyware and elections for hire
summary:
NSO Group, an Israeli company, sells the Pegasus phone-hacking spyware only to governments. In Spain, Pegasus was found on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's phone and on the defence minister's, and the government said it had not authorised this. A 2021 media investigation reported that Morocco selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones as targets, including politicians and senior officers. It also linked Morocco to President Macron's number. Algeria cut relations with Morocco, and Morocco denies using Pegasus.

In the United States, a federal court found NSO liable for hacking WhatsApp's servers to plant spyware on about 1,400 users' phones. The US Commerce Department has placed NSO on a trade blacklist.

In Kenya and Nigeria, foreign firms worked on presidential campaigns. Cambridge Analytica, a British data company, ran Uhuru Kenyatta's campaigns in Kenya and wrote his party's manifesto. In Nigeria it worked with Team Jorge, an Israeli hacking group, to discredit the opposition candidate. Team Jorge's leader later showed undercover reporters access to the Telegram account of William Ruto's digital strategist in Kenya.

In Madagascar, Mozambique and Zimbabwe, people tied to the Russian businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin worked on elections. In Madagascar his strategists dealt with several presidential candidates, and one said they gave him cash. Facebook removed fake account networks tied to Prigozhin that targeted eight African countries. In Zimbabwe, a Prigozhin-linked group sent its own election observers.

The firms get paid contracts, and their government clients get information on opponents and help for preferred candidates. These cases came out through undercover filming, forensic checks of phones, a leaked list of numbers and Facebook's takedowns.
implications: A politician, journalist or military officer whose phone is hacked can have their contacts, plans and private life read by a foreign government. Voters in Kenya, Nigeria and Madagascar chose between candidates whose messaging was shaped by paid outsiders working in secret. Election observers who are paid by a foreign businessman can give a flawed vote a clean report. The WhatsApp attack infected phones in 20 countries through an ordinary calling app.
uncertain: Morocco denies that it used Pegasus, and the client behind the Spanish infections has not been identified. Andry Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate in Madagascar. Kenyatta's party said it hired Cambridge Analytica's parent company only for branding.

title: Scam compounds and casino money inside Asian states
summary:
In Cambodia, people close to the ruling family are tied to firms the United States accuses of fraud and money laundering. Chen Zhi, born in Fujian in China, took Cambodian citizenship in 2014 and built the Prince Group into one of the country's largest conglomerates. He served as an adviser to Hun Sen, the interior minister and the National Assembly president. In October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him and called him the head of a cyber-fraud business.

Huione Group is a financial firm in Phnom Penh. Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, is a major shareholder and director of its payment arm, Huione Pay. Cambodia's central bank revoked Huione Pay's licence in March 2025. Two months later the US Treasury said Huione Group had laundered over $4 billion in illicit money.

In the Philippines, the state gaming regulator licensed offshore gaming operators, known as POGOs, from 2016. They were Chinese-run online gambling firms serving players in China. Senate hearings in 2024 tied many of them to fraud, trafficking and torture.

Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban in Tarlac, was linked by senators to a POGO hub raided in her town. The Ombudsman removed her from office, and a court later jailed her for life. A court also issued arrest warrants for Harry Roque, a former spokesman for President Duterte, and dozens of others for human trafficking over a hub in Pampanga. Prosecutors say Roque helped that hub seek a licence.

President Marcos ordered all POGO operations to stop by the end of 2024, and Congress then passed the Anti-POGO Act.

The firms got licences, local office-holders and payment channels. These cases came to light through Senate hearings, police raids, a US indictment and a US Treasury finding.
implications: People held in scam hubs faced trafficking and torture, according to the Philippine Senate hearings. When a mayor or a relative of the prime minister is involved, victims and their families have fewer safe places to complain. Money taken from scam victims abroad can pass through payment firms with owners tied to the government. In the Philippines, the ban closed the licensed industry and officials have been charged. In Cambodia, the main actions so far have come from the central bank and from the United States.
uncertain: The charges against Chen Zhi and Harry Roque have not been tried. The US Treasury finding on Huione is an administrative decision by one government, not a court verdict.

title: Iran's armed allies inside governments
roles: Where they sit in the state
summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards, through their foreign branch the Quds Force, back armed groups that hold posts inside other states. In Iraq, a 2016 law made the Popular Mobilization Forces part of the armed forces, paid from the state budget. The PMF is about 67 mostly Shia armed groups, almost all backed by the Revolutionary Guards. Kata'ib Hezbollah, which the US lists as a terrorist group and which operates under the Revolutionary Guards, staffs three PMF brigades. The PMF chairman, Falih al-Fayyadh, stayed in post after the US sanctioned him over the killing of protesters. In Lebanon, Hezbollah, a Shia party with an armed wing aligned with Iran, chose the health and labour ministers in the government formed in 2025. Its ministers walked out when the cabinet approved the aim that only the state hold weapons, and its leader rejected disarmament. The US sanctioned two of its sitting MPs in 2019. In Syria, Quds Force officers commanded alongside Bashar al-Assad's forces from 2012. When Assad fell in December 2024, Iran evacuated its commanders. In Gambia, a 2019 OCCRP investigation showed that a Lebanese businessman the US names as a Hezbollah financier was one of President Yahya Jammeh's closest associates and held the fuel supply monopoly. In Paraguay, the US sanctioned former president Horacio Cartes and the sitting vice-president in 2023, saying both had ties to Hezbollah members. Those sanctions were later lifted. Iran gets armed forces paid from other states' budgets, seats in cabinets and money from trade monopolies. These arrangements came to light through laws, sanctions decisions and journalists' investigations.
implications: In Iraq, taxpayers fund brigades run by a group that operates under another country's Revolutionary Guards. In Lebanon, the cabinet cannot decide alone on war and peace, because a party sitting in it keeps its own weapons and refuses to give them up. In Gambia, the country's fuel came through a monopoly given to the president's associate, whom the US names as a Hezbollah financier. Syrians lived for twelve years with Iranian officers commanding inside their army's garrisons.
uncertain: Two Iranians convicted in Kenya in 2013 over explosives were alleged, not shown, to be Quds Force members. The US sanctions on Paraguay's former president and vice-president were one government's decision, and they were later lifted.

title: Private forums where officials meet money
summary:
In Greece, Finland, Sweden, Estonia, Poland, Germany and Britain, sitting leaders or ministers attended the Bilderberg Meeting in 2024 or 2025. Bilderberg is a yearly private conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics. No public record is kept of what is said. Five sitting European Commissioners and NATO's secretary general, Mark Rutte, were on the 2025 list. The World Economic Forum, which runs the Davos meetings, named the prime ministers of Thailand and Montenegro to its Young Global Leaders programme while they were in office.

In the United States, authors of Project 2025, a governing plan published by the Heritage Foundation think tank, now hold senior posts. They include the budget office director and the chair of the communications regulator. The Federalist Society, a network of conservative lawyers, helped choose President Trump's judges, and most of his first appeals-court nominees were members. ALEC, a group of state legislators and companies, writes model bills for state legislatures. Earlier, under President Jimmy Carter, his national security adviser and secretaries of state and defence were members of the Trilateral Commission, a forum of business and political leaders.

In Argentina, President Javier Milei won a prize from a partner of the Atlas Network, which links free-market think tanks, before he entered politics. In New Zealand, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour worked for an Atlas partner in Canada. Members of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market academic society, have held office in Britain, Germany, Italy, the Czech Republic, New Zealand and Sri Lanka.

These groups get private time with officials, and some get people who share their views into office. Most of this is public, through attendance lists, membership records and leaked model bills.
uncertain: No court or inquiry has found that Bilderberg, the World Economic Forum or the Mont Pelerin Society directed any official's decisions. Membership is documented, and influence on particular decisions is mostly inferred. Trump's 2025 claim that the Federalist Society's former leader 'controls' judges is his own accusation, not a finding.

confirmed_by.title: Christian Science Monitor, 1980, on Trilateral Commission members in the Carter administration
ALEC Exposed (Center for Media and Democracy), 2011

implications: Voters cannot know what their leaders discussed with company heads at private meetings, because no record is kept. When one legal group helps pick most of a president's judges, its views can shape court rulings long after that president leaves. When a group of companies drafts model bills, state laws can carry their wording without voters knowing who wrote it. Belonging to these groups is lawful, and attending a meeting is not wrongdoing. It does give organisers access to officials that ordinary citizens lack.

summary:
In Brussels, Belgian prosecutors charged European Parliament vice-president Eva Kaili with corruption after police found bags of cash at her home. They allege that Qatar and Morocco paid to influence the Parliament, partly through a human-rights charity. In a separate case, prosecutors allege that associates of a former Huawei lobbyist paid MEPs to sign a letter opposing limits on Chinese 5G equipment. A British court jailed former MEP Nathan Gill for 10 years for taking money to make pro-Russian statements.

At UN climate summits, the hosts appointed oil-industry figures to lead the talks. Leaked papers showed that COP28 president Sultan Al Jaber, head of the UAE's state oil company, was briefed to raise its business in meetings with foreign governments. COP29's chief executive was filmed discussing oil and gas deals.

In Interpol, the UAE gave its foundation about $54 million, and a senior UAE interior official, Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, then served as president. French prosecutors opened an inquiry into torture complaints against him. China's vice-minister of agriculture, Qu Dongyu, heads the UN Food and Agriculture Organization in Rome.

In Washington, a law firm's inquiry found that World Bank leaders pressed staff to raise China's ranking in its business report. In Geneva, the Gates Foundation is one of the WHO's largest funders and earmarks most of its money. Leaked documents show Philip Morris campaigned to weaken the WHO tobacco treaty.

In The Hague, a former Mossad director pressed the International Criminal Court prosecutor before she opened a Palestine investigation, according to a press investigation.

The outside interests get favourable votes, softer rules and silence on their own conduct. These cases came out through police raids, leaked papers, press investigations and commissioned inquiries.
uncertain: Eva Kaili and the MEPs in the Huawei case are charged, not convicted. Kristalina Georgieva denies pressing staff over the China ranking. Attending the Bilderberg meetings, as NATO's Mark Rutte and five European Commissioners did, is lawful and is not evidence of wrongdoing.

implications: Decisions that affect everyone, such as climate targets, tobacco rules, police alerts across borders and war-crimes cases, can be shaped by the governments and companies they are meant to regulate. People who fled a government may find that government's officials sitting in the body that circulates arrest requests. When a private foundation earmarks its money for its own programmes, a health agency's priorities can tilt toward them. Residents of EU countries are bound by laws that some of their representatives were paid to influence.

title: Movements that sought the state itself

countries.note: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir.
The army said in January 2012 it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir.

summary:
In Sudan, Egypt, Tunisia, Morocco and Libya, parties from the Muslim Brotherhood tradition took power or won elections, and most were later removed or jailed.

In Sudan, Omar al-Bashir took power in a 1989 coup organised with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, a movement derived from the Brotherhood. Bashir admitted his role at his trial after his fall. The US has sanctioned Sudan's current finance minister, Gebreil Ibrahim, and an Islamist militia that has supplied up to 20,000 fighters to the army.

In Egypt, Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, won the presidency in 2012. The army removed him a year later, and the government declared the Brotherhood a terrorist organisation in December 2013.

In Tunisia, the Ennahda party led governments after winning the 2011 election. Its leader, former parliamentary speaker Rached Ghannouchi, has been in prison since 2023 and received a further 22 years. Ennahda calls the case political.

In Morocco, the Brotherhood-linked PJD led the government for ten years. In Libya, a member of the Brotherhood's party chaired the High Council of State in Tripoli for five years.

In Jordan, the Brotherhood's party, the Islamic Action Front, won 31 of 138 seats in 2024 and became the largest party. The government banned the Brotherhood's activities in April 2025. In January 2026 the United States listed the Egyptian, Jordanian and Lebanese branches as terrorist groups.

Hizb ut-Tahrir, a party that calls for a single caliphate, tried to recruit army officers. A Pakistani military court convicted a brigadier and four majors in 2012. The Bangladesh army said that year it had stopped a coup plot linked to the group.

These movements sought to govern through elections and, in Sudan, through a coup.
uncertain: Ennahda and Morocco's PJD say they have no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood. The Tunisian 'plotting against state security' case and the UAE's 2013 trial of Islah members are disputed by the accused.

confirmed_by.title: Egyptian cabinet designation, 25 December 2013
Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012

implications: Voters for these parties have seen them win office and then be banned. In Egypt, Brotherhood membership is punishable by up to five years in prison. In Jordan, the largest party in parliament comes from a movement whose activities are now banned. In Sudan, Islamist militias fight beside the army against the Rapid Support Forces, which affects any return to civilian rule. In Austria, police searched about 60 addresses over suspected Brotherhood networks, and a court later ruled the searches unlawful.

title: Lodges inside police forces and courts
summary: Freemasons and other lodges have had members among police officers, judges and generals, and some countries now make officials declare membership. Membership of a lawful lodge is not wrongdoing. In London, the Metropolitan Police made Freemasonry a declarable association in 2025. By February 2026, 397 officers and staff had declared membership, and the High Court refused the United Grand Lodge of England permission to challenge the rule. Britain has required new police officers, prosecutors and prison staff to declare membership since 1998. In Romania, a magazine reported in 2019 that the interim interior minister and the head of the Gendarmerie had joined lodges without declaring it, as it said the law required. In Italy, P2, a lodge led by Licio Gelli, had 195 military officers on its 1981 membership list, including the heads of all three intelligence bodies. Courts convicted Gelli and intelligence officers of planting false evidence to mislead the inquiry into the 1980 Bologna station bombing. Appeal judges, in a verdict made final in 2025, called Gelli the knowing financier of the bombing. Italy banned secret associations in 1982. In 2018 a Rome court convicted members of a group called P3 under that law for seeking influence over judges and state appointments. In Cuba, the former Grand Master of the Grand Lodge admitted in 2011 that he was a state-security officer placed there so the government could monitor Freemasons. In Gabon, the police chief removed in 2012 was grand master of a lodge. In Fruitland Park, Florida, a deputy police chief and an officer tied to the Ku Klux Klan left the force in 2014. These cases came to light through parliamentary inquiries, seized membership lists, court cases and journalists.
uncertain: The 2021 Daniel Morgan panel found no evidence that Masonic links were used corruptly in that murder case. A claimed secret lodge of Italian judges, 'Loggia Ungheria', was dismissed, and the lawyer who described it was sent to trial for slander. Gelli and others were acquitted of conspiring against the state through P2.

confirmed_by.title: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary, 1997; Freemasonry in Public Life, 1999
Italian Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on Freemasonry, December 2017

implications: Where police officers or judges belong to a lodge and do not say so, people in court cannot know whether those handling their case share a membership with the other side. Declaration rules, such as the Met Police rule from 2025, let complainants and managers check. In Blackburn in 1988, a father and son assaulted at an event of a lodge made up mostly of police officers were charged instead of their attackers. A jury acquitted them, and they later settled a false-arrest claim.

title: French lodges and African presidencies
roles: Head of state or minister in a lodge
case_role: Head of state or minister in a lodge

countries.note: The Grande Loge Nationale Française and the Grand Orient de France sponsored or chartered lodges in former colonies; the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009. Jacques Foccart's Service d'Action Civique ran France's African networks from the Élysée.

summary:
In Gabon, Congo-Brazzaville, Cameroon, Chad and other former French colonies, presidents and ministers have belonged to Masonic lodges or orders tied to French ones. Freemasonry is a lawful society with private meetings and ranks.

In Gabon, Omar Bongo founded the country's two grand lodges and led them until he died in 2009. The head of the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF), a French lodge, then installed his son Ali Bongo as grand master, the same year Ali became president. After the 2023 coup removed Ali Bongo, the head of the Grand Orient de France, France's largest lodge, reportedly met coup leader Brice Oligui Nguema in secret and offered support. In Congo, President Denis Sassou-Nguesso is reported to lead a grand lodge linked to the GLNF.

Jeune Afrique, a Paris weekly, reported in 2012 that the presidents of Burkina Faso, Mali and Guinea led or oversaw their national grand lodges. It also named Côte d'Ivoire's prime minister and interior minister, and Senegal's former president Abdoulaye Wade, as members. In Cameroon, Le Monde reported in 1999 that President Paul Biya gave tens of millions of francs to OSTI, a French Templar order. Some of that money moved from the state oil company. In Liberia, lodge membership was widely treated as a requirement for high office until the 1980 coup.

French lodges get access to African heads of state. The presidents get a private set of contacts in France. In France itself, lodges supplied files used to block Catholic army officers' promotions in 1901–04. A Gaullist militia founded by de Gaulle's Africa adviser was dissolved in 1982. Most of this comes from French and African press reports, not court cases.
uncertain: Most memberships rest on press reports, mainly Jeune Afrique in 2012, and several presidents have not confirmed them. No court has found that a lodge directed a government decision in these countries. Senegal's president Macky Sall denied the membership his opponents claimed.

confirmed_by.title: Jeune Afrique, investigation of Freemasonry in Africa, 2012
Le Monde, 1999, on payments to the Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique

implications: When a president and his ministers belong to the same private society, decisions can be discussed in meetings that parliament and the press cannot see. Citizens cannot tell whether an appointment, a contract or French backing came through official channels or through lodge contacts. In Cameroon, money from the state oil company reportedly went to a foreign religious order instead of the public budget. Ordinary lodge members are not accused of anything, and membership by itself breaks no law.

title: Banks and banking families
summary:
In Argentina, two former JPMorgan bankers run the economy ministry and the central bank. Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, worked at Goldman Sachs for 13 years before leading two central banks. In New York, the regional Federal Reserve Bank that supervises Goldman was led by a former Goldman economist. One of its examiners said she was fired after reporting gaps in Goldman's conflict rules.

In Lebanon, a study found that most major commercial banks had large shareholders linked to the political class. Those banks lent heavily to the state and the central bank. In Portugal, Ricardo Salgado, former head of the family bank Banco Espírito Santo, is on trial with former prime minister José Sócrates.

In Sweden, the Wallenberg family holds just over half the votes in Investor AB, which owns stakes in Ericsson, ABB and the defence maker Saab. In Russia, the US Treasury called Bank Rossiya the personal bank for senior officials, owned by people close to Vladimir Putin. In Ukraine, the state took over PrivatBank, owned by Ihor Kolomoisky, after a multi-billion-dollar hole was found.

In Basel, the Bank for International Settlements, which is owned by central banks, hosts central bank governors at closed meetings every two months. Carroll Quigley wrote that central bankers aimed to build a private world system of financial control, with the BIS at its apex. He also wrote that firms tied to J.P. Morgan and Lazard funded British policy groups after 1925.

Several popular claims about banking families are not supported by evidence. The claim that the Rothschilds or other Jewish banking families control governments, central banks and wars dates from the 1840s and is an antisemitic conspiracy theory. The US Federal Reserve, often named in it, is run by a Board of Governors appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. The claim that Nathan Rothschild profited from early news of Waterloo first appeared in an 1846 French pamphlet. Kuhn, Loeb's records show that Jacob Schiff refused to lend the Bolsheviks money. Quigley himself wrote: 'I never called it a conspiracy'.
implications: When former bankers run economy ministries and central banks, decisions on debt, wages and bank rescues are made by people who know the lenders' side best. In Lebanon, the banks that lend to the state are partly owned by people linked to the politicians who decide its borrowing. Ukrainians paid for PrivatBank's rescue with public money backed by IMF loans. Mozambicans and Malaysians repay debts that bankers arranged through bribes. In Sweden, one family's votes decide who sits on the boards of major employers.
uncertain: Carroll Quigley's account of a private world system centred on the BIS is his own interpretation and is not confirmed by other evidence in these cases. Whether Olaf Scholz's meetings with M. M. Warburg's owner affected Hamburg's decision to drop a tax claim is not proven. Cardinal Becciu's conviction ended in a mistrial.

title: Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network

countries.note: Rhodes's trustees, Milner, the Round Table journal (from 1910), Chatham House (1920) and the Pilgrims Society's London branch. Members held the posts of War Cabinet minister (Milner, 1916–18), the prime minister's private secretary (Philip Kerr, 1916–21) and editor of The Times (Geoffrey Dawson, 1912–19 and 1923–41).

Milner was High Commissioner from 1897. After 1902 his young staff ran the Transvaal and Orange River Colony administrations and worked for the 1910 Union. Patrick Duncan, one of them, became Governor-General in 1937.

The Council on Foreign Relations, founded in 1921 after the 1919 Hotel Majestic agreement in Paris, and the Pilgrims Society's New York branch (1903). The CFR's War and Peace Studies project sent memoranda to the State Department from 1939 to 1945.

summary:
This explains where today's Anglo-American foreign-policy institutes, Chatham House in London and the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) in New York, came from.

In South Africa from 1901, Alfred Milner, the British High Commissioner, hired young Oxford graduates to run the conquered Boer republics. This group, known as Milner's Kindergarten, held posts such as Transvaal Treasurer and town clerk of Johannesburg. Its members campaigned for the union of the four colonies, which became the Union of South Africa in 1910.

In Britain, Milner joined Lloyd George's War Cabinet in 1916. Philip Kerr, founding editor of the group's journal The Round Table, became the prime minister's private secretary. Geoffrey Dawson, Milner's former secretary, edited The Times during the years of appeasement.

In Canada, two Governors General, Earl Grey and John Buchan, came from the circles of Cecil Rhodes and Milner. The movement set up groups in Australia and New Zealand as well.

In 1919 Lionel Curtis, a Kindergarten member, convened the Paris meeting that led to Chatham House. During the Second World War its research service was moved into the Foreign Office.

In the United States, the CFR ran confidential postwar planning for the State Department during the war, paid for by the Rockefeller Foundation. Allen Dulles, who led one of its study groups, later became Director of Central Intelligence. A 1977 study found that more than half of the senior US officials it surveyed for 1945–72 were CFR members.

Much of the account of a single group comes from the historian Carroll Quigley. He described a secret society founded by Cecil Rhodes. The offices these men held are public and documented.
uncertain: The claim that these men formed one secret society rests mainly on Carroll Quigley's books. From 1970 writers such as Gary Allen and G. Edward Griffin recast his account as a world conspiracy of international bankers, and Quigley rejected that reading. The documented part is a set of lawful clubs and public appointments.

confirmed_by.title: Carroll Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (written 1949, published 1981)

implications: Today's foreign-policy institutes in London and New York grew out of this group. They gave a small number of men from Oxford, merchant banks and Wall Street law firms regular contact with ministers and officials. Their members wrote papers that governments used, such as a CFR memo on Greenland that reached President Roosevelt in 1940. Many of their members later held the offices that made foreign and military policy. Membership of these bodies is lawful.

title: The anticommunist web, 1945–1990

countries.note: Gladio, disclosed by Prime Minister Andreotti on 24 October 1990, and P2, whose 1981 list held the heads of all three intelligence services. Italy is where the stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most.
The Chilean intelligence service DINA under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting of Operation Condor in Santiago in November 1975.
CIA support for the stay-behind networks is confirmed in the Italian and Belgian inquiries; Condor's 1976 bombing of Orlando Letelier in Washington was carried out by DINA agents.

summary: This explains where some of today's arrangements came from: between 1945 and 1990, anticommunist secret armies, lodges and military governments worked together across borders. NATO countries set up secret 'stay-behind' groups of armed civilians, called Gladio in Italy, to act if the Soviet Union invaded. Italy's prime minister disclosed its group to parliament in 1990. Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland exposed or disbanded theirs soon after. Turkey's unit sat inside the army's Special Warfare Department. Switzerland's full report on its secret army, P-26, is sealed until 2041. In Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia and Peru, military governments ran Operation Condor, a joint plan to seize opponents across borders, many of whom disappeared. Secret police files found in Paraguay in 1992 proved it existed. Courts in Argentina, Uruguay and Italy have since convicted former presidents, ministers and officers. In Italy and Argentina, the P2 lodge listed ministers, generals and intelligence chiefs as members. They included Argentina's navy commander and a welfare minister whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad. Silvio Berlusconi, later Italy's prime minister for three terms, was on its list. In Greece, members of IDEA, a secret officers' society, led the 1967 coup. In Turkey, a 1996 car crash showed a deputy Istanbul police chief, an MP and a Grey Wolves gunman wanted by Interpol travelling in one car. The interior minister had signed the gunman's gun licence. The sponsors got armies, police and intelligence services ready to act against the left. These facts came out through parliamentary inquiries, police archives and trials.
uncertain: Rome courts acquitted Gelli and others of conspiring against the state through P2. Brazil's armed forces deny taking part in Operation Condor. The claim that Greece's stay-behind unit seized the Defence Ministry in the 1967 coup rests on historical accounts, not a court finding.

confirmed_by.title: European Parliament resolution on Gladio, 22 November 1990
Belgian Senate parliamentary inquiry on stay-behind networks, 1991
US National Security Archive, Operation Condor briefing books

implications: In Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and Italy, families of the dead and disappeared waited decades for verdicts, and many accused died first. Pinochet died without being convicted. Courts are still ruling on events of that period, such as the Bologna bombing verdict made final in 2025. In Switzerland, citizens cannot read the full report on their own secret army until 2041. Italy's 1982 ban on secret associations came out of this period and prosecutors still use it.

countries.note: BCCI secretly owned First American Bankshares in Washington through nominees; former Defense Secretary Clark Clifford, its chairman, was indicted in 1992 (charges dropped for ill health). The CIA held accounts at BCCI.

summary:
This explains where today's ways of hiding money in banks came from. Two banks of the 1970s and 1980s served governments, spy services and criminals.

In Italy, Banco Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982 with about $1.3 billion missing. Much of it had moved through offshore companies tied to the Vatican Bank, its main shareholder. Its chairman, Roberto Calvi, belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge whose seized membership list named ministers, MPs and generals. Calvi was found hanged in London in 1982. The Vatican Bank paid creditors but denied legal liability. Italy's top court ruled that the 1929 treaty with the Vatican shielded the bank's president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, from Italian courts. Ambrosiano branches in Peru, Nicaragua and the Bahamas lent to governments and shell companies.

BCCI, the second bank, was mostly owned by the Abu Dhabi government by 1991. A US Senate inquiry found that it secretly bought First American, Washington's largest bank, while the Federal Reserve was told it was not involved. BCCI held deposits from the central banks of Peru and Paraguay. In Panama it held a large account for General Manuel Noriega and paid off the mortgage of his chosen presidential candidate. In Jamaica it handled most government foreign-currency accounts. It paid the debts of Bert Lance, President Carter's former budget director. The Senate found the CIA kept using BCCI after it knew the bank was a criminal enterprise.

The banks got deposits and protection, and officials got loans, payments and hidden accounts. The cases came to light through the 1982 collapse, the 1991 closure of BCCI and the trials and inquiries that followed.
uncertain: Who killed Roberto Calvi is unknown: an Italian forensic report said he was murdered, but five defendants were acquitted in 2007. Robert Altman, First American's president, was acquitted, and the state case against its chairman Clark Clifford was dropped because of his health. Cardinal Angelo Becciu's 2023 Vatican conviction over a London property later ended in a mistrial.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate, The BCCI Affair (Kerry–Brown report), 1992
Bank of Italy inquiry into Banco Ambrosiano, 1981–82
Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking (Stewart), 1983–85

implications: Depositors and taxpayers carried the losses when these banks failed. In Peru, about three-tenths of the government's cash reserves sat at BCCI. Officials who kept money or took loans at these banks could avoid checks at home. The same methods are still used: offshore companies, banks in small jurisdictions, and treaties that keep some institutions outside national courts. The Vatican now tries its own financial officials, and its court convicted a former Vatican Bank president of embezzlement in 2021.

title: Sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed

countries.note: Every prime minister and state president from D. F. Malan (1948) to F. W. de Klerk (1989–94) was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918. Its membership list was published by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978.

Army officers who later founded the Black Hand killed King Alexander Obrenović in 1903 and its leader, Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis', became head of military intelligence; its rival, the White Hand, put General Petar Živković in power as prime minister in 1929.
IDEA, a secret society of army officers, prepared the April 1967 coup; the colonels ruled until 1974 and were tried in 1975.

The Society of St. Tammany ran New York City's Democratic machine; the Know Nothings won Massachusetts in 1854; the 1920s Klan elected governors in Indiana, Colorado and Oregon and helped send Hugo Black to the Senate and then the Supreme Court.

summary:
This explains where today's arrangements came from. In South Africa, every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society. A 1979 report found that all but two cabinet ministers were members, as was the chief of the defence force.

In Greece, members of IDEA, a secret officers' society, led the 1967 coup. Courts later convicted the junta's leaders of high treason. In Serbia, officers who went on to found the Black Hand killed the king and queen in 1903. A rival officers' group, the White Hand, later supplied a prime minister of Yugoslavia.

In Canada, the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, supplied four prime ministers and most Toronto mayors for over a century. In Ireland, the Taoiseach John A. Costello and other ministers belonged to the Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic order.

In the United States, the Ku Klux Klan backed or supplied governors in Indiana, Colorado, Alabama and Oregon in the 1920s. Hugo Black, a former Klansman, joined the Supreme Court. In Massachusetts, a secret nativist order won the governorship and almost every legislative seat in 1854, then passed laws aimed at Irish Catholics.

Carroll Quigley wrote that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society and named Alfred Milner its leader. Milner's posts as High Commissioner in southern Africa are documented.

The societies got jobs, contracts and laws for their members. Their membership came out through published lists, journalists and trials.
uncertain: Several membership claims rest on single reports or later books, such as the Thule Society lists and the Saskatchewan Klan's role in the 1929 election. Carroll Quigley's account of Rhodes's secret society is his own interpretation. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke called lists that name Hitler as a Thule member spurious.

confirmed_by.title: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)
Greek junta trials, 1975
Indiana and Colorado Klan histories; Hugo Black's radio address, 1 October 1937

implications: In South Africa, apartheid laws were made by a cabinet drawn almost entirely from one secret society, and the officials who carried them out came from the same body. Catholic voters in Massachusetts and Oregon faced laws aimed at their schools. In Florida, two police officers tied to the Klan were removed in 2014, and their past arrests were reviewed. Where one society fills a police force or civil service, people outside it may find that appointments and enforcement favour its members.
