summary:
This explains where today's government-funded democracy grants, such as those of the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), came from. From the late 1940s to 1967, the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) secretly paid for student, labour, cultural and broadcasting groups abroad.

In Germany, the CIA funded Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, which broadcast from Munich into the Soviet bloc, until 1971–72. In France, the Congress for Cultural Freedom was run from Paris by a CIA officer. It had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines.

In the United States, the CIA paid for the international programme of the National Student Association. It also set up the Asia Foundation in 1954 as a CIA company. The Senate's Church Committee found CIA money in nearly half of the international grants made by a group of US foundations in 1963–66.

In Italy, CIA money went through the American Federation of Labor's Free Trade Union Committee from the 1948 election onward. In Brazil, the CIA-linked Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action paid for opposition candidates in the 1962 elections. A Brazilian parliamentary inquiry investigated it, and President Goulart closed it the next year.

The funding came to light through press reports in 1966 and 1967 and the Church Committee inquiry. Congress created NED in 1983 and funds it through yearly appropriations. Its founder said in 1991 that much of its work had been done covertly by the CIA 25 years earlier.

NED gave about $2 million to the Nicaraguan opposition before the 1990 election, about half of it to La Prensa. Russia banned NED as 'undesirable' in 2015, and China sanctioned it in 2019.
uncertain: Russian and Chinese claims that NED is an intelligence front are their governments' assertions, and no independent body has upheld them. What the Brazilian trainees of the US-funded labour institute AIFLD did in the 1964 coup remains unclear, according to the historian Cliff Welch.

confirmed_by.title: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), Final Report, Book I, 1976

Ramparts, March 1967

implications: Groups that take money from a foreign government can be shaped by the donor's aims. In Italy, Brazil and Nicaragua, US money went to one side before national elections. Readers of the Congress for Cultural Freedom's magazines and listeners to Radio Free Europe did not know the CIA paid for them until the 1960s and 1970s. Today the Russian and Chinese governments cite NED grants when they ban or sanction foreign-funded groups. Russia's ban on NED was the first under its new law on 'undesirable' organisations.

summary: This explains where some of today's arrangements came from: from the 1950s to the 1980s, US-funded programmes trained the economists who later ran several countries' economies. In Chile, US government aid and then the Ford Foundation paid for 126 Chilean students to train in economics through a link between the University of Chicago and Santiago's Catholic University. Their plan, known as 'El ladrillo', became the military government's economic programme in 1975. Graduates then held the economy, finance and planning ministries and the central bank under Pinochet. Sergio de Castro was finance minister for six years. Miguel Kast became central bank governor in 1982. In Indonesia, the Ford Foundation paid for University of Indonesia economists to take graduate degrees at the University of California, Berkeley. After Suharto took power in 1966 he made them his economic team. Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS for 16 years and wrote the five-year development plans. Ali Wardhana was finance minister for nearly 15 years. In Saudi Arabia, a joint commission set up in 1974 and co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary ran US technical help to the government. A 1979 US Government Accounting Office report found it was paid for almost entirely from a Saudi account at the US Treasury and that it recycled oil money. The United States got economic ministries run by people it had paid to train. These links came out through the governments' own appointments and official audits.
uncertain: John Perkins says his firm, Chas. T. Main, inflated growth forecasts so that countries such as Indonesia would take large loans. This rests on his own account in a 2004 book.

confirmed_by.title: US General Accounting Office report on the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, 1979
New York Times, 'Economic Hit Man' review, 2005

implications: In Chile, the Chicago-trained ministers ran the economy under military rule until the 1982 debt crisis ended de Castro's term. In Indonesia, the same small group wrote the national development plans for more than 15 years, also under military rule. In Saudi Arabia, the government paid for US advice from its own oil income held at the US Treasury. People in these countries lived under economic plans made by officials trained abroad and appointed by governments they had not elected.

summary:
This explains how today's arrangements usually come to light and how often the findings are later undone. In South Africa, the Zondo inquiry found in 2022 that ministers and heads of state companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family. In Denmark, an internal review found that military intelligence let the US NSA tap cables, which the NSA used to wiretap Germany's chancellor Angela Merkel. In Switzerland, it came out in 2020 that the CIA and Germany's BND had secretly owned Crypto AG. That firm sold encryption machines to more than 120 governments.

Turkey dismissed about 150,000 public employees after 2016 and seized 784 companies it called Gülen-linked. Sudan's transitional government dismissed judges appointed under Omar al-Bashir, and a court ordered some of them back in 2021. The Philippines banned offshore gaming firms after Senate hearings in 2024.

In Brazil, Lula's corruption convictions were annulled in 2021. In Turkey, the top court overturned 275 Ergenekon convictions in 2016, saying there was no evidence the group existed. A Milan court acquitted Eni and Shell over a Nigerian oil block, and a Panamanian court acquitted the founders of Mossack Fonseca, the firm in the Panama Papers.

The US designated Colombia's president Gustavo Petro under its drug order in 2025, and Colombia rejected it, though no court has heard the case. Zimbabwe's Kuda Tagwirei became a cabinet minister in 2026 while under US and UK sanctions. Andrej Babiš became Czech prime minister again in 2025 after an EU audit found he had a conflict of interest.
uncertain: Many cases rest on one government's sanctions, such as US designations of Colombia's president and Haiti's former president Michel Martelly, which no court has heard. The Mossack Fonseca acquittal rested on insufficient and improperly gathered evidence. The Eni and Shell acquittal also ended the case without a finding of bribery.

confirmed_by.title: Italian Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982
Turkish Constitutional Court and Court of Cassation rulings on Ergenekon and Sledgehammer, 2015–16

implications: For people living in these countries, a sanction or commission report shows what a government or inquiry concluded, not what a court proved. Officials named by an inquiry may be acquitted, have convictions annulled, or return to office. Purges can also sweep up people with no proven link: Turkey removed judges and police by decree without individual trials. When courts throw out cases because evidence was gathered illegally, as in the Ergenekon case, the original accusation is neither confirmed nor cleared.
